newsitem.title: THAILAND: FOCUS - Thai central bank moves to ease jitters.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Thai central bank moves to ease jitters.

text.p: The Bank of Thailand unveiled a state-run deposit insurance scheme on Friday as it tried to calm market jitters over the stability of commercial banks and finance firms after suspending 58 cash-strapped finance companies since late June.

Assistant central bank governor Siri Garnjarerndee said the central bank also asked Thai and foreign banks, as well as other operating finance firms, to lend surplus funds to institutions facing public runs on their deposits.

Siri's statement was designed at stopping heavy withdrawals of funds from some small Thai banks and finance firms in the past two days after the central bank told 42 finance firms to stop operating for at least three months.
"The measures are adopted to protect sound financial institutions from the lack of public confidence...no institutions can survive if they are hit by public runs," he said.
Investors were sceptical about government assurances since Tuesday that no additional financial institutions would be closed by the authorities.
Thailand's 91 finance companies have faced severe liquidity problems arising from growing non-performing loans extended to a collapsed property sector.
Siri said the deposit insurance scheme, which he hoped would be necessary for only about two years, was in line with policies of the International Monetary Fund (IMF).
Thailand on Tuesday announced an IMF-sponsored austerity package to reform its economy which is growing at its slowest in over a decade.

Siri said the central bank's Financial Institution Development Fund (FIDF) would guarantee bank deposits up to a maximum of three percentage points above the average three-month fixed deposit rate of five top Thai banks.
For funds deposited at finance firms, it would cover up to six percentage points above the average three-month fixed rate.

Siri said the FIDF would also guarantee loans extended to operating institutions by other corporate creditors but only up to four percentage points below the average minimum lending rate (MLR) of five top Thai banks.
He said finance firms suspended earlier could benefit from the deposit insurance scheme if they could rehabilitate themselves in the future.
The FIDF may float government-run bonds to raise funds for financing the deposit insurance scheme, Siri said. Sound banks and finance firms would be asked to contribute more to the plan.

Siri said to prevent any closure of financial firms facing public runs on deposits, banks and firms benefiting from the inter-company shifts of funds were asked to set aside half of the windfall funds for relending to those suffering from the shifts.

He said surplus banks and institutions would charge FIDF an interest rate of 1.5 percent above the central bank's seven-day bond repurchase rate. FIDF will then charge corporate borrowers facing a short-term liquidity squeeze an interest rate equal to 1.5 percentage points above its cost of funds.
The central bank expected what it called the fund recycle measure to be in effect for only one month, after which market jitters should ease.
Siri said 19 foreign banks with full branches in Thailand were among main recipients of the shifted deposits within the Thai money market in the past month.
"I am disheartened to hear about a trend that foreign banks are being perceived by Thais as being more secure than Thai banks," he said.
